newsitem.title: UK: Factory discharges "feminising" fish in Britain.
newsitem.headline: Factory discharges "feminising" fish in Britain.

text.p: Textile and electronic factories are releasing high levels of "gender-bending" chemicals into Britain's rivers to cause sex changes in male fish, the New Scientist weekly said on Thursday.

Researchers from the Scottish Environment Protection Agency (SEPA) believe that 11 rivers in southern and central Scotland could contain up to 10 times the proposed limit for nonylphenol, a chemical that can feminise fish.
Nonylphenols, so-called gender-bending chemicals, are used to wash grease from sheepswool fleeces and to clean circuit boards and phthalates -- used in softening plastics.
"Male fish exposed to effluent containing these chemicals start producing a protein called vitellogenin, which is usually present only in females," the magazine said.
A report published last year found the highest levels of nonylphenols in the River Aire in northern England, downstream from several wool factories.

Geoff Brighty of the Environment Agency said proposed limits for nonylphenol could also be breached downstream of factories in England and Wales. "That is where we shall be focusing our investigations," he told the New Scientist.
SEPA's Gerry Best said his agency was already in discussions with the industry to replace gender-bending chemicals with safer alternatives.
